newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Labour's Clark seeks early signal from NZ First.
newsitem.headline: Labour's Clark seeks early signal from NZ First.

text.p: Opposition Labour Party leader Helen Clark on Friday said New Zealand First leader Winston Peters held the key to the outcome of Saturday's election and should indicate quickly who he was negotiating with.
"Mr Peters holds the key... and he has been pretty cagey," Clark said in a radio interview.

"Making up his mind is going to have to come in the next week or so and he will need to indicate whether he is negotiating with Mr Bolger or with me. In fact he may... start negotiating with both of us early next week."

New Zealanders vote in a general election on Saturday, and on current polling a deal between Labour and economic nationalist New Zealand First with the support of the left-wing Alliance is seen as the most likely outcome.

Discussing differences between Labour and New Zealand First, Clark said accepting the compulsory private superannuation scheme proposed by New Zealand First, rather than Labour's eight cents in the dollar targeted tax, would eventually lead to a surcharge on the basic pension, and Peters "had not thought his way around that yet".
Asked about the future of the Reserve Bank Act, Clark said Labour did not think the Act should be changed.

"We have consistently said its objectives should be price stability, but if we are asked, well do you agree overall with Mr Peters that macroeconomic policy should be about sustainable economic development,' we say yes, of course.
"And that is why you need an economic policy that consists of more than just adherence to the Act."

She said the conservative National government has put very heavy reliance on the Act and it was almost impossible for Reserve Bank Governor Don Brash to keep inflation in its 0-2 percent target band without "strangling the economy".
"The economy has been strangled, growth has been strangled, interest rates are through the roof, the dollar is up and it's very difficult for exporters and anyone with a mortgage.

"Our approach has been to say: leave the target of the Act as price stability, widen its target to enable them more flexibility in management of monetary policy and in addition address the factors driving inflation such as the skills
shortage, the unanticipated booms in the property market in Auckland which came from immigration surges in the past couple of years. Let's do something about low income housing."

Labour has said it would widen the 0-2 percent band to minus one to three percent, but New Zealand First wants to keep inflation below the average inflation rate of New Zealand's main trading partners and add sustainable economic growth to the bank's price stability target.
Clark said Labour's policies were likely to prevail in a left wing government because the Alliance on the left and New Zealand First on the right would tend to balance each other.
She said New Zealand First was asking for somewhat less spending than Labour and the Alliance somewhat more.

With that kind of lineup, with the Alliance positioning itself to our left and New Zealand First to our right it may well be... the policy mix Labour has settled is the most coherent and substantial."
